genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the silversmith avoids setting gems at the end of the day because her hands tremble
her mother practiced the same craft in front of her during her childhood
watching her mother decided her choice of trade
the lack of fine tools in the family workshop forced her to improvise
she smoothed her pieces with a hide stretched over a wooden block
that early constraint gave her great patience
her work is known to be sturdy and free of scratches
her refusal of short deadlines lengthens the queue of her customers
she maintains that haste always leaves a mark in the material
text: Her hands shake a little once the light goes, and that is the reason behind a rule the silversmith set for herself early on: she never seats a stone after dusk. As a child she watched her mother tip a blade across warm metal, and that sight settled what she would do with her life. The family workshop held no fine tools, so she learned to bring up a shine with a hide stretched over a block of wood, and the slowness of it built a patience few people carry. Those lean beginnings explain the name she earned later on: her mounts hold fast and her surfaces come away unmarked. She turns down hurried orders, so the line of buyers keeps stretching, and the wait only sharpens what people feel for her work. Metal punishes hurry, she says, and every flaw you can see began in a moment when somebody tried to outrun it.

units: the product is criticized because it sets too early
a dry mark shows up on wide surfaces and can no longer be removed
the thinner evaporates too fast in heated rooms
the maker advises adding an additive that slows the drying
this additive does not weaken the strength of the final coat
he also advises laying it on in thin overlapping bands
tests on hardwood confirm the improvement
the scraping tool has to be sharpened before every coat
the overall judgment is mixed and depends on the willingness to change one's practice
text: The complaint raised most often against this varnish is how early it sets. Spread over a wide panel, it starts to pull while the brush is still traveling, and it leaves a dry edge that nothing will lift out afterward. Bench testing shows why: the thinner flashes off far too fast in a heated room. The maker answers on two fronts. A retarder, stirred in at a low proportion, stretches the working time without weakening the cured coat. The second answer is about the hand rather than the can, since the varnish wants narrow overlapping bands instead of broad sweeps. Trials on hardwood panels bear the gain out, provided the scraper is honed before every coat goes on. So the judgment stays split. Here is a demanding product, dependable for anyone ready to rebuild a habit, and a letdown for anyone who wants a result on the spot.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop recommended by the reader
the rods are sorted before the weaving in this place
the pieces made there keep their shape once dry
the pace was faster in the previous workshop
the pieces from the previous workshop lost their shape quickly
the former teacher merely showed a movement to be copied
the present teacher breaks down every motion and allows mistakes
the writer progresses more slowly but remembers more
the difficult operations are carried out in silence in this new workshop
text: I am writing from the basketry workshop you pointed me to, and I want to set down what marks it off from the last one. Here the rods are sorted before anybody starts weaving, and that one precaution changes the whole result, because the baskets hold their curve once they have dried. In the house I left, the pace ran faster, yet the pieces went out of shape within a week. The teaching parts ways as well. My old master would show a figure once and wait for me to copy it; the master here breaks every motion apart and lets me fail without stepping in. I move ahead more slowly and I hold on to far more. The feel of the room differs too, since the delicate operations are carried out in silence, while the other workshop hummed with talk throughout. Thank you for sending me here. With my respectful regards.

units: three qualities are named as conditions for entering this trade
the folding tool must be handled without stiffening the joint
a tense wrist makes the fold run off true
the shades of the covering materials must agree whatever the surrounding light
the sequence of operations for the rounded spine cannot be altered
workshops state that the training has no set length
a beginner's progress is described as uneven
practitioners name the freedom of the hand among the rewards
mending a damaged object brings a satisfaction the practitioners mention
text: What is asked of anyone who wants a bench in a bookbinding workshop? Three aptitudes come back in the masters' answers. The first belongs to the hand, since the folder is held without locking the wrist, and a tight wrist sends the crease off at a slant. The second belongs to the eye, because the shades of leather and cloth have to agree under a weak lamp as readily as under a bright one. The third is a memory for movement, since a rounded spine grows out of a run of steps whose order will bear no shuffling. And the training, how long does it run? The workshops answer that it has no set end, and that a careful beginner climbs in uneven jumps. What does such a demanding road hand back? Binders name the freedom of the hand, the range of the commissions, and the pleasure of putting a battered volume back into use.

units: the beginner turned up before the agreed hour
he asked for permission to handle the cutting tools
the craftsman refused and gave him a cleaning job
the request came back seven days later
the craftsman then handed him a metal plate and asked for a straight line
the line that came out went off course
the craftsman corrected the position of the tool and of the finger without comment
the next day's line was distinctly better
the craftsman played the success down by mentioning how many lines are needed
he quietly admitted that he had done worse at the same age
text: The apprentice turned up ahead of time and asked the engraver whether he was allowed to touch the burins. The master said no, not yet, and handed him a broom, laughing as he did so. A week later the apprentice put the same question again. That week the engraver laid a copper plate on the bench and told him to try one straight line, nothing beyond that. The line he cut ran off sideways. The master passed no comment at all; he only showed how to tilt the tool and where the thumb belongs. The next day the apprentice cut a line that was nearly clean, and he bragged about it. One line does not add up to a trade, the engraver told him, and he would want thousands of them before he talked that way. Then he added, lower down, that his own line had been the worse of the two at that age.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the spread of trading routes drove orders beyond what the workshops could handle
the craftsmen changed the technique for bending the boards
round hearths replaced heating one piece at a time
several boards were softened at once
the vessels that came out had identical measurements
the traders could work out the size of their loads in advance
disagreements over the quantities carried grew fewer
the rise in demand called for more young people in training
the trade bodies made entry into the craft harder
the fear of the craft weakening produced a codification of the movements
text: Once the trading routes widened, the cooperage workshops watched orders pile up beyond anything they could honor. That pressure pushed the coopers to rethink the way they bent their staves. Rather than heating one piece at a time, they raised round hearths where a dozen boards went supple together. The change carried a result nobody had looked for. Since the casks now came off the bench at matching sizes, traders could reckon their loads before the goods were even carted, and the wrangling over delivered quantities died away. Uniform sizes fed the demand, and the demand called for more apprentices than the trade had ever taken on. The trade bodies tightened their rules of entry, uneasy at the thought of the craft thinning out. From that unease grew the long codification of movement that the workshops held on to afterward.

units: an uneven surface takes up color unevenly
dark patches appear instead of a smooth fade
wood cut across its fibers drinks more of the product
the correction rests on a graded run of abrasives
you begin with a coarse abrasive that removes the ridges left by the tool
no intermediate grit may be skipped
each abrasive removes only the traces of the one before it
the final smoothing follows the direction of the fibers
wetting the wood before the last pass raises the fibers so they can be knocked down for good
text: A rough surface drinks stain unevenly, and the maker who waves that detail away finds dark blotches where he had wanted a soft, even fade. The fault sits in the fiber itself. Cut across, it opens and swallows three or four drops where the flat grain takes only one. The cure is a patient climb through the grits, taken in order. You start with a biting abrasive that shears down the ridges the blade has left. Move on to a middling grit, then a fine one, and skip no stage along the way, since each paper wipes out nothing but the scratches of the paper before it. Polish at the end along the run of the fiber, and damp the wood before the final pass, so the whiskers that stand up are laid down for good. The surface then goes silky under the palm, and the stain settles across it at one even tone.

units: two cutting edges were shown to a doubting beginner
the first edge was ground to a narrow angle
it produced long shavings in a soft wood
it buckled on meeting a hard patch of the wood
the second edge had a wider angle
it damaged the soft fiber and left an uneven bottom
it crossed the hard patches without harm
the conclusion drawn is that a tool can only be judged against its use
the narrow angle is kept for finishing passes
the wide angle suits the fast removal of material
text: Two blades set side by side on the bench did more for the trainee's doubts about angles than any argument would have. The first, a plane iron ground to a narrow bevel, bit into the soft wood and threw off unbroken shavings, yet it buckled the instant it ran into a knotty stretch. The second, ground much blunter, tore the soft fiber and left a ragged floor, while it crossed the same knot without flinching. The shop drew its lesson: a tool is worth nothing away from the job it was made for. So the keen bevel is kept for finishing, where the thickness taken off is counted in slivers, and the stout bevel for hogging off waste, when the bulk to be shifted outweighs the state of the surface. The trainee boiled the rule down his own way: you pick an angle against the material, not against your neighbor.

units: four supplies must be gathered on the working surface
the suppleness of the rods is checked by a bending test
rods that are too stiff must soak for about sixty minutes
the assembly starts with eight rods crossed into a star
the center is held down with the finger during the weaving
each pass must be drawn tight against the one before it without pulling sideways
the upright rods are then raised to form the sides
the evenness is checked by holding the piece at eye level
the top rim is folded inward then held by a stitch
the drying is done flat and away from any heat source
text: Before you begin, lay out on the bench the following supplies: a bundle of softened fibers, a curved needle, a length of waxed thread, and a pair of straight-bladed shears. Bend a strand to make sure it gives without cracking; if it holds stiff, put the bundle under water and leave it for an hour. Move on to the base. Cross eight strands into a star, pin the center under your thumb, then weave, drawing every pass tight against the one before it and never hauling from one side alone. Carry on with the walls. Bring the uprights up one by one and run the weave round in a spiral, checking the evenness at eye level. Close with the rim. Cut the strands on a slant, fold the uprights inward, and stitch the edge with the waxed thread. Dry the piece flat, well clear of any heat source.

units: a demonstration open to the public takes place in a forge of an old district
the craftswoman lit her fire and announced her program to the public
the metal brought to a high temperature was bent with the hammer
the onlookers watched the colors of the piece change
the piece was cooled in a tub
a file served to even out the surface
the craftswoman stressed that sturdiness does not rule out finishing
children were invited to hold the gripping tool
a weekly evening opening was announced
the neighbors will be able to follow the making of a grille
text: A crowd of onlookers presses up against the forge in the old district, where a public demonstration has just got under way. Early in the afternoon the farrier lit her hearth and told the crowd what she meant to turn out. An hour on, the bar came glowing out of the coals and took its curve under measured hammer blows. The watchers saw the piece run from white to brown, then blacken in the quenching tub. The smith next picked up a file and brought the surface smooth, remarking that strength is no excuse for skipping the care. Towards the close of the afternoon she asked the youngest ones to hold the tongs while she struck. The session ended on an announcement: the workshop will open its doors one evening a week, so that the neighborhood can follow the making of a balcony grille.
